title: 3-Read Friday #89: Lesson Planning, Dual Coding, and Multi-Stranded Curriculum
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #89 is a curriculum-and-cognitive-science issue built around three arguments for structural change. Dr Dario Emanuele, whom Barton names his "new favourite Substacker," argues novice teachers should be given high-quality, already-planned lessons rather than asked to plan from scratch before they know what a successful lesson even looks like. David Didau then dismantles a popular oversimplification of dual coding theory, explaining when adding visuals to teaching actually helps and when it becomes noise. Dylan Kane closes with an account of restructuring his scheme of work into multiple parallel strands rather than sequential units, aimed at giving the hardest topics more time to consolidate. Barton also flags Book 7 of his Tips for Teachers series, on Responsive Teaching.
points: Barton's unusually strong endorsement of Emanuele ("my new favourite Substacker") signals this issue's structural theme -- his piece argues for giving novice teachers pre-planned lessons rather than requiring them to plan from scratch before mastering classroom basics.
Didau's dual coding piece directly counters a common CPD oversimplification, explaining precisely when integrating visuals with text helps memory and when it fragments it.

Kane's multi-stranded curriculum redesign addresses a structural problem shared with Emanuele's piece -- both argue the standard unit-by-unit sequencing of teaching, whether of lessons or curriculum content, doesn't give the hardest material enough time to consolidate.
Read together, the issue's throughline is structural reform to teacher training and curriculum design, rather than individual classroom technique.
quotes: Dr Dario is my new favourite Substacker. Read this post for a compelling argument for why we need to give novice teachers high-quality, already planned lessons.
When Dual Coding was all the rage a few years ago, every PowerPoint slide had to be accompanied by a visual representation, no matter how tenuous.
David dives into Dual Coding research to examine when integrating text and images is useful.
One for the maths geeks. Dylan outlines how he has changed the format of his scheme of work this year, why he did so, and offers practical tips for anyone wishing to try this approach too.
Before we begin, you may want to check out my brand-new 16-part book series, The Tips for Teachers guide to. Book 7 on Responsive Teaching is now available.
